title: Metabolic activation of nitroarenes and Nrf2-Keap1
text: Air pollution will increase because of extreme weather. Its particulate phase contains nitroarenes that arise from car and diesel exhaust and may contribute to lung cancer. We will show that a major stress response pathway leads to nitroarene activation with resultant modifications in proteins and DNA that lead to mutation. Measurement of these changes will increase exposure assessment and lead to improved biomonitoring and lung cancer prevention.

title: Changing Oceans Affect Shellfish Toxins
text: Harmful algal blooms (HABs) of the dinoflagellate Alexandrium spp. threaten coastal populations of humans and wildlife in Alaska. Toxins produced by Alexandrium can accumulate in shellfish and other filter feeders and at high concentrations and cause paralytic shellfish poisoning (PSP). In response to community concerns regarding the safety of shellfish harvest Southeast Alaska Tribal Ocean Research (SEATOR), a network of coastal tribal communities, created a robust and expansive monitoring program for HABs, shellfish toxins, and ocean acidification (OA). A major concern for coastal Alaskan communities is how environmental conditions will affect the safety of subsistence shellfish harvest. Warming sea surface temperatures, air temperatures, and increasing acidity have the potential to alter production of toxins by Alexandrium and increase the potential bloom window into seasons not typically associated with HABs. This uncertainty will be addressed in this project using a multi-faceted and rigorous approach. Aim 1 will leverage long term monitoring data from SEATOR (n=3,433 shellfish samples), in situ environmental measurements, remote sensing products, and traditional ecological knowledge to generate machine learning and mixed effects harmonic models predicting shellfish toxins from environmental variables. Congener specific data generated in Project 2 will also be analyzed for species specific and spatial trends in association with environmental variables. Aim 2 will analyze 919 discrete OA samples collected by coastal communities paired with 1,814 previously analyzed discrete samples to investigate spatiotemporal relationships between OA parameters (i.e. pCO2) on shellfish toxin dynamics. Using OA parameters constrained from Aim 2 and environmental data from Aim 1, Aim 3 will use in vivo experimentation to examine the effects of changing ocean conditions (temperature, pCO2) on toxin accumulation and maximum toxicity in subsistence shellfish species. This project creates an important linkage between empirical models of HABs and shellfish toxicity and environmental conditions, creating outputs of HAB dynamics which are actionable and will be shared with tribal partners and communities.

title: RNA-Binding Proteins and RNA-Dependent Proteins - An Emerging Role for RNAs in Plasmodium Biology
text:
The Apicomplexa is a phylum of diverse obligate intracellular parasites infecting humans including Plasmodium, the
causative agent of malaria. In this application, we aim to decipher the role of RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) and RNA-
dependent protein (RDPs) in the parasite biology and validate their potential as novel targets for antiparasitic strategies.

title: LISTOS for Cancer Control - Leveraging Implementation Science To Optimize Strategies for Cancer Control
text: LISTOS Narrative: Our proposed project, LISTOS for Cancer Control (Leveraging Implementation Science To Optimize Strategies for Cancer Control) will increase capacity for implementation research and practice in cancer prevention and control. The project proposes to establish a new center and carry out two cancer control implementation research projects: 1) Implementing colorectal cancer screening in publicly funded health systems, and 2) Implementation of integrated care for rapid diagnosis of breast cancer. The research projects and capacity building activities have the potential  to advance the science of cancer control implementation and reduce the burden of cancer.

title: Peripheral Artery Disease: Long-term Survival & Outcomes Study (PEARLS)
text:
Peripheral artery disease (PAD) is a common and highly morbid condition that is a major cause of disability and
associated with a high risk of heart attack, stroke and death. We propose to develop a large cohort of PAD
patients identified using a novel method and follow them over time to better understand the trajectory of survival
and clinical outcomes in these patients, assess the impact of existing treatments on patient outcomes and
uncover racial disparities in care and outcomes. Our work will advance PAD research and provide important
insights regarding how best to improve PAD care.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Clinical Decision Support for Preventing Hypoglycemia in Hospitalized Patients
text:
For the 1 in 5 patients hospitalized with diabetes, hypoglycemia, the most common adverse side effect of
insulin, can be life-threatening. This research expands upon previous work to use artificial intelligence to
predict and prevent hypoglycemia. The goal is to develop a clinical decision support tool for use in the
electronic health record that increases the safety of care for patients with diabetes.

title: Neural Circuit Mechanisms of Seizure Susceptibility in a Mouse Model of Angelman Syndrome
text:
Epilepsy is a common, life-altering condition, as one in ten people will experience at least one seizure in their
lifetime. Completion of the proposed research will advance our understanding of the neural circuit mechanisms
underlying seizure susceptibility in a mouse model of Angelman syndrome, a severe neurodevelopmental
disorder in which refractory epilepsy is common. The information gained could inspire the rational design of new
anti-epileptics for individuals with Angelman syndrome, and possibly other neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Gradient biomaterials to investigate niche regulation of hematopoiesis
text:
The body’s full complement of blood and immune cells are generated from a small number of hematopoietic
stem cells (HSCs) in regions of the bone marrow termed niches. Niches provide matrix, metabolic, and cell-cell
communication signals that influence HSC activity and which evolve over time in response to ageing and
disease. The proposed research will develop a tissue engineering model of niche remodeling to selectively
expand HSCs ex vivo for therapeutic and experimental applications.

title: The Genetic Basis of Virulence in Cryptococcus Neoformans
text:
Isolates of the fungal pathogen Cryptococcus can vary greatly in their propensity to cause
morbidity and mortality. This research will advance public health by identifying dif-
ferences in genes and gene networks that underlie variation in disease related traits for
three species of Cryptococcus. A deeper understanding of how genetic variation inﬂu-
ences virulence traits may lead to new approaches for the treatment and prevention of
cryptococcal disease.

title: Monitoring Human Exposome with Extracellular Vesicle Tricorder
text:
Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are shed into the bloodstream by all cells in the body, providing a unique opportunity
to monitor the health impact of environmental exposures through liquid biopsies. Here we propose a technology
framework integrating bulk and single EV omics, nanotechnologies, and microtechnologies to extract the blood
fingerprints of organ-specific biological responses to life course experiences. The proposed methodologies,
technologies, as well as data sets, will be of high value to both basic and translational research communities.

title: Elucidating Molecular Drivers of Aging and Alzheimer's Disease via Multimodal Imaging Mass Spectrometry
text:
This application proposes to map cellular and molecular alterations
associated with normal aging and Alzheimer’s disease in brain tissue using imaging mass spectrometry
in tandem with various forms of microscopy, multiomic spatial profiling, and machine learning. We
hypothesize that comprehensive multimodal molecular imaging and analysis of brain tissues will
provide a deeper mechanistic understanding of understudied neuropathologies, contributing to the
complexity and heterogeneity of Alzheimer’s disease, including cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA),
dystrophic neurites, neuropil threads, granulovacuolar degenerating bodies, and gliosis . This work will
generate high spatial resolution and comprehensive molecular atlases of normal aging and Alzheimer’s
human brains and our advanced data analysis strategies will further reveal disease
state/transition/class-specific molecular signatures, provide insight into key molecular pathways along
with changes or disruption across tissue regions of interest, and identify potential disease subgroups.

title: Reprogramming T cell function with multiplexed genome engineering to develop next-generation immunotherapy
text: Adoptive T cell therapy has demonstrated lasting clinical responses in hematologic malignancies, but relapse and the suppressive tumor microenvironment remain critical barriers. This project addresses these gaps by precisely regulating synthetic receptor dynamics in T cells and developing novel protein chimeras for targeted degradation, offering innovative strategies to advance cancer immunotherapy.

title: Entorhinal-hippocampal interactions during progressive memory impairments in mouse models of Alzheimer's disease pathology
text:
Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a debilitating disorder that causes severe memory impairments, but it remains
unclear the specific memory circuits and mechanisms that break down to impair cognition. The medial
entorhinal cortex is an early site of pathology and thus may also be an important site of circuit dysfunction that
contributes to cognitive deficits. This proposal will characterize how medial entorhinal and hippocampal circuits
break down during the progression of memory deficits in three well-validated mouse models of AD pathology.

title: Sequencing Core
text: Sequencing Core Summary The mission of the HIPC program at LJI is to use hypothesis-free approaches to define comprehensive molecular profiles of T cell subsets in the context of lung pathogens. The areas of interest cover an extremely wide spectrum of “omics” analysis including: (i) analysis of global gene expression (bulk and single-cell RNA-seq), (ii) analysis of T cell receptors high variable sequences repertoire by bulk or single-cell TCR-seq, (iii) analysis of changes in global epigenetics profiles (genome-wide enhancer profiles) using single-cell ATAC-seq, in T cell memory subsets from patients infected and/or vaccinated against, SARS-CoV-2, Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), and other lung pathogens. All these “omics” applications rely on standardized and well-validated high-throughput Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS) methods – a key service provided by this Core. The Sequencing Core will support all NGS activities for all the three projects involved in this program. This will be facilitated by the extensive genomics expertise of its personnel and the availability of cutting-edge technologies and automated platforms to generate highly reproducible and robust sequencing data from a large number of samples. Practically, the Sequencing Core will interface directly with all three Projects and provide a standardized and quality-controlled pipeline consisting of receiving samples, sorting cells, preparing RNA/DNA, preparing libraries for high-throughput NGS, and transferring the resulting data to the Data Management and Analysis Core for subsequent analysis.

title: Merging Sound and Light: Dual-Mode Ultrasound/NIR Fluorescence Imaging with Metal-Doped Graphene Quantum Dots
text:
This work focuses on the development of novel doped graphene quantum dots (GQDs) as dual-mode
contrast agents for ultrasound and fluorescence imaging, addressing limitations of modern diagnostics.
By offering deeper tissue visualization, improved stability, and cost-effective production, GQDs have the
potential to improve diagnostic for such conditions as cancer and cardiovascular disease among others.
This technology is portable, scalable and cost-effective, which can help increase imaging accessibility,
and promote personalized medicine in healthcare settings with infrastructure limiitations.

title: TULP3 integrates essential ciliary functions
text:
The primary cilium is a tiny, extracellular-facing organelle, with a distinct composition from that of the rest of the cell 
or plasma membrane, that coordinates diverse extracellular signals (i.e odorants, metabolites, light, neuropeptides, 
hormones) and converts them into coordinated cellular responses. Though primary cilia have been implicated in a 
number of pathologies including ciliopathies, diabetes, neural disorders, disrupted immunity, and cancer, the 
mechanisms by which cilia are built and process signals remain poorly understood. The goal of this proposal is to 
explore the role of the ciliary traffic protein TULP3 in coordinating both making a cilium and maintaining receptors 
inside the cilium and how understanding these functions applies in the biological context of immunity.

title: Deciphering the Enhancer Landscape and Regulatory Code of Heart Development at Single-Cell Resolution
text:
This project aims to decipher the enhancer landscape and regulatory code of heart development at single-cell
resolution. By mapping and validating enhancer activity and using deep learning models, the research will
provide critical insights into the gene regulatory mechanisms underlying heart development and congenital heart
disease. The results will advance our understanding of non-coding genetic variation in heart disease and lay the
foundation for precision tools in cardiac research and therapeutics.

title: Pediatric Bone Marrow Failure Network (pBMFN) - Admin Core
text: Project Summary / Abstract – Administrative core The Pediatric Bone Marrow Failure Network (pBMFN) is a partnership between the North American Pediatric Aplastic Anemia Consortium (NAPAAC) and the Rare Diseases Clinical Research Network (RDCRN) formed with the goals of developing optimal approaches to clinical care, promoting career development, developing resources for the clinical, research, and patient communities, and fostering clinical trial readiness for children with BMF. The complexity of coordinating the multiple pBMFN projects and cores integrated with the RDCRN Data Management and Coordinating Center (DMCC) and patient advocacy groups, and supporting the participating study sites requires a well organized administrative structure. With the objective of coordinating and supporting the activities of the pBMFN, the Administrative Core of the pBMFN, headquartered at Boston Children’s Hospital, has been organized to fulfill the following responsibilities: 1) provide overall administration for the pBMFN including scientific conduct, policies, procedures, and fund allocation, 2) coordinate activities and communications between the pBMFN, the RDCRN, RDCRN DMCC, NAPAAC and Patient Advocacy Group, 3) coordinate and supervise activities of the pBMFN study sites, 4) provide biostatistical support in partnership with the RDCRC DMCC for pBMFN research, 5) provide data informatics support in partnership with the RDCRN DMCC to ensure best practices for rigorous validated data collection and data monitoring, 6) work with the RDCRN DMCC and Career Enhancement Core to develop the pBMFN website and communications for outreach and education including sharing the goals and achievements of the pBMFN, career enhancement opportunities, and awareness of pBMFN resources, 7)coordinate sample shipments and centrally process, log and bank bio- samples, 8) participate in RDCRN efforts to synergistically develop resources and methodologies for collection and sharing of clinical and laboratory data including harmonization of common data elements, 9) develop infrastructure and procedures to foster clinical trial readiness and participation. The Administrative Core leverages the robust institutional infrastructure at Boston Children’s Hospital to support regulatory guidance, biostatistics/bioinformatics support, experienced administrative support, and clinical research support. The Administrative Core is the central hub facilitating collaboration, coordination, and communications between all the pBMFN and RDCRN teams and patient advocacy groups, as well as coordinating regular input from the External Advisory Committee. The impact of the Administrative Core lies in enabling and facilitating successful attainment of the pBMFN goals to improve diagnosis and treatment for pediatric BMF.

title: Role of MMP3 in cardiac microvascular barrier dysfunction and heart failure during sepsis
text:
We propose to investigate the crucial role of MMP3 in mediating cardiac microvascular barrier dysfunction and
heart failure during sepsis. Our aim is to identify the B1R-MMP3 pathway as a novel therapeutic target for treating
sepsis-induced heart failure, a leading cause of death in sepsis patients. Our findings will establish a new paradigm,
providing deeper insights into the mechanisms of sepsis-induced myocardial edema and heart failure, while
potentially revealing new therapeutic strategies to improve sepsis treatment and survival.

title: Mechanisms of Ion Channels and Enzymatic Membrane Proteins
text:
This research program aims to discover the three-dimensional structures and to understand the fundamental
mechanisms of two classes of proteins that reside within cellular membranes: ion channels and enzymatic
membrane proteins. The ion channels under study regulate the flow of potassium, calcium, and chloride across
cellular membranes and they are thereby involved in cognition, neuronal signals, muscle contraction, cellular
motility, fluid secretion and a host of other processes; the enzymatic membrane proteins under study catalyze
crucial post-translational chemical reactions in the cellular construction of signaling molecules (such as
hormones and protein signaling complexes) that act to control cell growth and cell differentiation in normal
tissues and can contribute to cancer progression when mutated or coopted by oncogenic signaling networks.
The molecular, structural, and functional principles obtained from the studies will provide fuller understandings
of the inner workings of these intricate protein machines and may inspire new approaches to intervene in
diseases that include cancer, cystic fibrosis, immune disorders, and obesity.
